steps.text: The Hall of the Two Truths. Egyptians believed that after death a person came before the gods to be judged. In Budge's translation Spell 125 is the chapter of entering into the Hall of Double Right and Truth, the hall now usually called the Hall of the Two Truths. Here the scribe Ani and his wife Tutu enter, bent forward in humility; above them twelve gods sit on thrones as the judges.
steps.pacing_note: No wait: the visitor moves on when ready.

steps.text:
The Declaration of Innocence. Egyptians believed the dead had to declare their innocence before forty-two divine judges, naming each one and denying one wrong to each. These are seven of Ani's forty-two declarations, in Budge's translation of 1895 (his numbers 2, 3, 4, 8, 12, 13 and 19). They are Ani's words: you are only reading them.
“Hail, thou who art embraced by flame, who comest forth from Kheraba, I have not robbed with violence.”
“Hail, Fentiu, who comest forth from Khemennu, I have not stolen.”
“Hail, Devourer of the Shade, who comest forth from Qernet, I have done no murder; I have done no harm.”
“Hail, thou Flame, which comest and goest, I have spoken no lies.”
“Hail, thou whose face is turned back, who comest forth from thy hiding place, I have not caused shedding of tears.”
“Hail, Bast, who comest forth from the secret place, I have not dealt deceitfully.”
“Hail, Sertiu, who comest forth from Annu, I have not been angry and wrathful except for a just cause.”
steps.pacing_note: No wait: the visitor moves on when ready.

steps.text: The scales. Egyptians believed the heart, the seat of thought and memory, was weighed against the feather of Ma'at: truth and right order. The jackal-headed Anubis tests the balance. The papyrus shows Ani's heart and the feather in balance, and in its text Thoth reports that the heart “hath been found true by trial in the Great Balance.”
steps.pacing_note: No wait: the visitor moves on when ready.

steps.text: Thoth records; Ammit waits. The ibis-headed Thoth, scribe of the gods, writes down the result. Behind him sits Ammit, the Devourer, with the head of a crocodile, the forepart of a lion and the hindquarters of a hippopotamus, “ready to spring forward to consume Ani's heart if he fails to pass the test” (the British Museum's description). Egyptians believed that a heart which failed would be consumed. The papyrus does not show that happening, and neither does this walkthrough: in its text the gods answer, “Let it not be given to the devourer Amemet to prevail over him.”
steps.pacing_note: No wait: the visitor moves on when ready.

steps.text: Horus presents Ani to Osiris. Found true, Ani is taken by the hand by the falcon-headed Horus, son of Isis, and led to Osiris, ruler of the dead, enthroned in a shrine with Isis and Nephthys behind him. Egyptians believed the justified dead passed on into the realm of Osiris. Horus says: “I have come unto thee, O Unnefer, and I have brought the Osiris Ani unto thee.”
steps.pacing_note: No wait: the visitor moves on when ready.
